query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled aging treatment applied to a non‐equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA (with density below 6 g/cm³) will drive the precipitation of stable intermetallic compounds. These intermetallics modify the alloy’s local chemistry and microstructure, thereby promoting the formation of a more protective passivating oxide film at high temperatures and in corrosive environments compared to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: A non-equilibrium, rapidly solidified or mechanically alloyed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy exhibiting a supersaturated solid solution with dispersed metastable phases.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to an aging (annealing) heat treatment at a controlled temperature and time under an inert atmosphere to promote the nucleation and growth of stable intermetallic compounds.
generation.conditions: Corrosion evaluation in a standard 3.5% NaCl solution at room temperature and high-temperature oxidation testing at a set temperature (e.g., 800 °C) in air. The sample size, geometry, and processing history are kept constant aside from the aging treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence and distribution of stable intermetallic compounds (e.g., Ti-rich or Mg-enriched phases) that arise during the annealing process.
generation.mechanism: The aging treatment releases the supersaturation of the as-cast alloy, resulting in the controlled precipitation of intermetallic phases. These phases alter the local elemental distribution at or near the surface. In turn, the modified chemistry encourages the development of a dense, adherent oxide layer (by preferential oxidation of elements with strong oxide-forming tendencies), which slows both corrosion and high-temperature oxidation kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the aged alloy will exhibit a more noble corrosion potential and a lower corrosion current density, as well as reduced weight gain during oxidation tests, reflecting improved passivation and oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: The initial non-equilibrium as-cast (or rapidly solidified) alloy state without the aging treatment.
generation.boundary: The alloy’s overall density remains below 6 g/cm³ and the processing methods (e.g., rapid solidification) that yield a metastable state are maintained. The aging treatment parameters (temperature and time) are controlled so that only the intended intermetallic precipitation is induced without full transformation to equilibrium phases.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvements in corrosion resistance and oxidation behavior is not precisely predictable due to the complex interplay among alloying element chemistry, processing variables, and intermetallic phase distribution.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples. Retain one set in the as-cast state (baseline) and subject the other set to the specified aging heat treatment. Quantitatively evaluate the microstructural evolution (using XRD and microscopy) to confirm the presence of stable intermetallic phases in the aged samples and then perform standardized corrosion (in 3.5% NaCl solution) and high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., at 800 °C).
measurements: Electrochemical corrosion potential and current density
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not show a statistically significant formation of stable intermetallic phases and consequent improvement (i.e., lower corrosion current density and reduced oxidation kinetics) relative to the as-cast baseline, or if they exhibit deteriorated performance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: We found that AlBeMgTiSi is the most energetically stable HEA, followed by AlBeMgTiCu and AlBeMgTiLi. Si is the most stabilizing constituent element, which greatly reduces the formation energy. Because of Si, the formation energy of AlBeMgTiSi is the lowest among the studied HEAs. AlBeMgTiLi is the lightest among the examined HEAs, followed by AlBeMgTiSi and AlBeMgTiCu. It was found that Li, Be, Mg and Al reduce the density in any HEA that contains them, and AlBeMgTiLi includes all of them. Amongst the considered HEAs, AlBeMgTiSi is not only the most stable alloy but also the one with the largest elastic modulus and specific stiffness, together with the highest Pugh’s ratio. We found that both Be and Si increase the elastic modulus and specific stiffness in any HEA containing them. The exceptionally low mass densities of the lightweight HEAs explain the remarkably high values of specific stiffness in comparison to the traditional HEAs. It was found that all the studied lightweight HEAs are likely brittle. The aim of the present work is to investigate the influence of systematic variations in Mg content on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion behavior of these alloys. By characterizing the resulting intermetallic phases, grain refinement, and passive film formation, this study identified how processing and composition synergistically affect the corrosion resistance and mechanical performance. This work offers new insights into the design of corrosion-resistant, high-strength materials and represents a novel extension of compositionally complex alloy design to Mg-rich systems.
